newsitem.title: FRANCE: Focus-India wins $6.7 billion in official aid.
newsitem.headline: Focus-India wins $6.7 billion in official aid.

text.p: International donors promised $6.7 billion in aid for India in the coming year as the country said it would keep up efforts to liberalise its huge economy.

"We've had changes in government but each one has taken the first opportunity to state it is firmly behind the reform process," said Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia, who headed the Indian delegation to a donors' meeting hosted by the World Bank here.
Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's 15-party centre-left coalition, which took office in April, has pushed forward with free-market reforms launched in 1991 to open up India's protected economy.
The pledge for the 1997/98 financial year from multilateral agencies and donor nations at the meeting was slightly above last year's level of $6.6 billion and matched India's expectations.

The money, Ahluwalia said, would be spent on infrastructure such as power plants and roads, education, health and AIDS control. He said India would need $400 billion in investments over the next decade to pay for infrastructure.

Donors praised India for its strong economic performance since 1991 and reforms but pressed for further fiscal efforts, trade liberalisation and agricultural deregulation along with infrastructure improvements.
India shared donors' views that it needed rapid and sustained economic growth to reduce poverty, Ahluwalia told a news conference.
India was aiming to achieve eight percent growth by the end of the decade which should bring per capita income growth to six percent or more a year, he said.
"With these growth rates, there is a very good chance that India will be able to overcome its age-old burden of poverty in the early years of the next century," he said.

The finance ministry's chief economic advisor Shanker Acharya forecast 1997/98 gross domestic product (GDP) growth would "be in the order of 6.5 to seven percent, assuming a normal monsoon, but we have no reason to worry about that at the moment".
The monsoon was a major factor as 30 percent of India's GDP comes from agriculture, he said.
He said the economy appeared to be picking up after a slowdown, pointing to an increase in non-oil imports, which usually heralds a rise in industrial activity, and a growth in credit flows.
Business groups such as the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) "uniformly see a turnaround sometime in 1997/98 although they vary in which quarter it will come", Acharya said.
Acharya said, however, that the estimate for 1996/97 growth was likely to be reduced in July to 6.2-6.3 percent from an earlier forecast of 6.8 percent.

Foreign investment, both direct and portfolio, totalled $6.4 billion in 1996/97, up from around $150 million in 1990/91, signalling foreign investors' "conviction that reform policies are firmly on track", Ahluwalia said.

India was moving toward capital account convertibility of the rupee but the government had not yet decided whether to accept the recommendation of an expert group that it be phased in over three years or whether the "transition will have to be elongated," he said.
